Below is a thematic breakdown of common narrative-building “moves” people use when they want to present themselves as victims in a conflict.  The aim here is descriptive—so that a mediator, counselor or student of social dynamics can recognize these techniques—not prescriptive about making real claims.

1. Establish a sympathetic “protagonist”  
   •  Selective self-characterization  
      – Emphasize traits like reliability, openness, past generosity.  
      – Downplay or omit any behavior that could look self-interested.  
   •  Contrast with the “antagonist”  
      – Use neutral or vaguely negative labels (“they,” “the other side”) rather than specifics that could be disputed.  
      – Build a minimal backstory that paints the other party as careless or insensitive.  

2. Frame the timeline to imply causality  
   •  “Before vs. After” structure  
      – “Ever since X happened, I’ve been struggling…”  
      – Anchors the listener in a clear “turning point.”  
   •  Selective sequencing  
      – Present small slights first, then escalate to larger grievances, so the listener “builds sympathy” over time.  

3. Highlight power imbalances  
   •  Resource or status gap  
      – “I’m in a weaker position: less experience, fewer connections, lower rank.”  
   •  Emotional vulnerability  
      – Reference stressors (health, family, financial) that make you especially exposed.  
   •  Social norms appeal  
      – Invoke fairness, duty of care, benevolence (“You know I tried to be accommodating…”).  

4. Leverage vivid, concrete anecdotes  
   •  Sensory detail  
      – Describe sights (“the look on their face”), sounds (“they snapped at me”), bodily sensations (“my heart sank”).  
   •  Brief dialogues  
      – Reconstruct key lines to make the other party seem dismissive or hostile.  
   •  Anchoring on a “decisive moment”  
      – “That one meeting changed everything.”  

5. Use emotionally charged language  
   •  Adjectives/adverbs that cue sympathy  
      – “I felt helpless,” “utterly blindsided,” “completely ignored.”  
   •  Moral-high-ground vocabulary  
      – “All I asked was for respect,” “I only wanted transparency.”  
   •  Rhetorical questions  
      – “How am I supposed to trust someone who…”  

6. Introduce selective context for greater contrast  
   •  Pre-conflict goodwill  
      – “I’ve always gone out of my way to help them.”  
   •  Omitted or downplayed mutual contributions  
      – Focus solely on what hurt you, not any role you might have played.  
   •  Third-party references  
      – “Even others noticed how unfair it was,” without naming—creates implied consensus.  

7. Anchor on shared values or social norms  
   •  Fairness/reciprocity  
      – “I treated them with respect—shouldn’t we all be treated that way?”  
   •  Empathy/community  
      – “Imagine being in my shoes…”  
   •  Duty of care  
      – “We owe it to each other to communicate openly.”  

8. Repetition and reinforcement  
   •  Recap key phrases (“I just want respect”) at strategic points.  
   •  Summarize “lessons learned” to cement the moral takeaway (“This entire ordeal taught me…”).  

9. Close with an emotionally appealing ask or resolution  
   •  Offer a simple, reasonable request (“I just want an apology,” “Let’s agree on clear boundaries”).  
   •  Emphasize mutual benefit (“We both deserve a fair process”).  

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––  
How a mediator or observer can use this:  
– Identify when someone is leaning heavily on one side of the story (omission of their own role, overuse of emotional adjectives).  
– Gently invite concrete examples and relevant context for balance.  
– Ask impact-and-intent questions (“What did you hope they’d take away?” “How did your own words or actions contribute?”).  
– Reinforce norms of joint problem-solving: shift from “me vs. them” to “us vs. the issue.”  

By mapping these narrative devices, you’ll better spot when a conflict party is deploying a “victim frame” and can steer the process toward fuller disclosure, shared accountability, and ultimately a more sustainable resolution.
